title: Preterite: completed past actions
explanation: Spanish marks the past inside the verb ending, not with a helper word. The preterite is for single, completed actions: -é/-aste/-ó for -ar verbs, -í/-iste/-ió for -er/-ir verbs.
example: Hablé con ella ayer. — 'I spoke with her yesterday.'
contrast: English needs 'did/spoke' as separate words; Spanish folds tense + person into one ending, so 'hablé' already means 'I spoke'.

title: Imperfect: ongoing or habitual past
explanation: The imperfect (-aba / -ía) describes the past as ongoing, repeated, or background — with no clear endpoint. It sits opposite the preterite's finished actions.
example: Hablaba con ella todos los días. — 'I used to talk / was talking with her every day.'
contrast: English blurs these into one 'talked'; Spanish forces you to choose whether the action was a completed event (preterite) or a background/habit (imperfect).

title: Ser vs estar: two verbs for 'to be'
explanation: Spanish splits 'to be' in two: ser for identity and inherent traits, estar for states, locations, and how things are right now.
example: Ella es alta. (trait) vs Ella está cansada. (state)
contrast: English uses one verb 'to be' for both; the ser/estar choice encodes whether you mean an essential quality or a current condition.

title: Gender agreement
explanation: Articles and adjectives change form to match the noun's gender and number: el gato negro, la gata negra, las gatas negras.
example: La casa blanca — 'the white house' (all three words carry feminine agreement).
contrast: English adjectives never change shape; in Spanish the whole noun phrase agrees, so the ending on 'blanca' is grammatical, not decorative.

title: Reflexive verbs with -se
explanation: A reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos) marks that the subject acts on itself. Many everyday routines are reflexive in Spanish: levantarse, ducharse, llamarse.
example: Me llamo Ana. — literally 'I call myself Ana' = 'My name is Ana.'
contrast: English rarely says 'myself' for these; Spanish uses the reflexive as the normal way to express routines and 'getting' into states.

title: Present subjunctive: the unreal / wished-for
explanation: The subjunctive appears after wishes, doubts, emotions, and certain conjunctions. The vowel 'flips': -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
example: Espero que hables español. — 'I hope (that) you speak Spanish.'
contrast: English mostly lost this mood; Spanish still grammatically marks that something is desired or uncertain rather than factual.
